property_summary: For any contract state, owner() returns the stored nonzero owner address (i.e. owner() == c.owner() == stored _owner), whereas the mutant returns address(0) whenever a nonzero owner is set — so the reference always reports the actual stored owner and the mutant misreports nonzero owners as zero.

For every input owner address set via transferOwnership, the reference contract's owner() returns the stored nonzero owner address, whereas the mutant sometimes returns address(0) when a nonzero owner is stored — so the general rule: after setting owner to any address A, owner() == A; the mutant violates this for some A (any nonzero).

For every address a set as the owner via transferOwnership (including nonzero addresses), the reference contract's owner() returns that stored address; the mutant falsely returns address(0) whenever a nonzero owner is stored, so there exists an owner address for which owner() differs.
For every address x passed to transferOwnership by the current owner, C.owner() returns that same address; the mutant sometimes returns address(0) instead when a nonzero owner is set.

For every address candidate 'newOwner' passed to transferOwnership by the current owner, the reference contract's owner() returns that stored owner address; the mutant incorrectly returns address(0) whenever the stored owner is nonzero, so there exist inputs (any nonzero newOwner) for which owner() differs.

For any non-zero newOwner address, transferOwnership on the reference contract always succeeds and sets owner() to that newOwner; the mutant that removes the non-zero check additionally allows transferring ownership to the zero address, which changes owner() to address(0) for that input (zero address) and thus violates the intended rule that owner() is never set to address(0).

The reference never allows ownership to become the zero address via transferOwnership(newOwner) (it reverts if newOwner == address(0)); the mutant removes that guard and thus permits setting owner() == address(0) for newOwner == address(0).

For all addresses newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract never sets owner() to the zero address (it reverts for newOwner == address(0)); the mutant removes that require and thus for newOwner == address(0) the mutant will set owner() == address(0), violating the rule.

The reference contract never allows transferOwnership(address(0)) — calls with any newOwner either succeed setting owner() to newOwner if non-zero or revert for zero; the mutant removed the zero-address check and thus for newOwner==address(0) it succeeds and owner() becomes address(0), violating the invariant that transferOwnership never results in owner()==address(0).

For any nonzero newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) always sets owner() == newOwner (reference); the mutant that passes _msgSender() into _transferOwnership instead will leave owner() as the caller for some newOwner inputs and thus violate this rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner in the correct contract; the mutant sets owner() to the caller instead, violating this property for some newOwner inputs.

For any nonzero newOwner and when called by the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner (the mutant sets owner() to the caller instead and so will violate this for some newOwner inputs).

For any caller who is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant incorrectly leaves owner() equal to the caller for some newOwner inputs.

For any caller that is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner in the reference implementation; the mutant instead sets owner() to the caller (msg.sender) causing owner() != newOwner for some newOwner inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and any non-zero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract changes the stored owner to newOwner (i.e. owner() == newOwner after the call); the mutant incorrectly blocks transfers when newOwner != current owner, so there exist inputs where calling transferOwnership should change owner but the mutant leaves it unchanged.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any non-zero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant prevents changes when newOwner != current owner, so for some newOwner values the mutant leaves owner() unchanged.

For any nonzero newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference always succeeds (does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant sometimes reverts (or prevents change) when newOwner != current owner, breaking this behavior.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract succeeds (does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant adds a guard requiring newOwner == current owner which makes some valid transfers either revert or be no-ops, violating this rule.

For any non-zero address newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) on the reference succeeds (does not revert) and results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant blocks transfers to any different address (requiring newOwner == current owner) causing the call to revert or be a no-op for some fuzzed newOwner values.

For every call, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual paused state (_paused), but the mutant returns the negation, so there exists inputs where paused()'s boolean differs (i.e., calling paused() after pausing/unpausing yields opposite results).

For every sequence of calls that sets the contract pause state (pauseDeposit/unpauseDeposit via keeper), the public getter paused() must reflect the internal _paused value (i.e., paused() == true iff contract is paused); the mutant returns the negation so there exist sequences (e.g., after pauseDeposit by keeper) where paused() differs.

For any keeper address, after invoking pauseDeposit() (when caller is keeper) the public paused() must report true; the mutant flips the boolean so for some keeper address the observed paused() will differ (false) and the test will fail.

For every address chosen as keeper and any caller, after the keeper calls pauseDeposit() the public paused() getter must return true (contract is paused); the mutant flips the boolean so paused() can return false after pauseDeposit(), violating the rule.

For every address chosen as keeper and any call sequence, the public paused() getter reflects the actual pause state (_paused) so paused() == true iff the contract is paused; the mutant returns the negation and thus for some keeper/call sequences paused() will differ.

For every input, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual _paused state (so calling paused() after pausing/unpausing reflects that state); the mutant that always returns true breaks this because it will report paused() == true even when the contract was unpaused.

For any caller and any pause/unpause sequence, the reference's paused() reflects the actual paused state (returns false after an unpause), whereas the mutant always returns true (so paused() == true even after an unpause) — thus there exists inputs (who calls unpause) that make the mutant disagree with the reference.

For any caller and any admissible timing, after the owner calls unpauseDeposit (so the contract is unpaused in the reference), paused() must return false; the mutant that forces paused() to always return true will disagree for some inputs where an unpause occurs.

For any address caller, after the owner unpauses the contract (via unpauseDeposit called by the keeper after executeBatchDeposit cooldown), the reference contract's paused() may return false (reflecting internal _paused), while the mutant that forces paused() to always return true will sometimes return true instead — so there exists inputs (keeper address and timing) where paused() differs between reference and mutant.

For any caller and any prior pause/unpause actions, the reference contract's paused() reflects the internal _paused state (can return false after an unpause), whereas the mutant that always returns true will sometimes report paused() == true when the reference reports false (i.e., paused() must not always be true).

For every input, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual paused state (true iff contract is paused after pause/unpause calls); the mutant always returns false so there exist inputs (sequences of keeper calls) where paused() differs (e.g., after pause() is called) and the mutant breaks the rule.

For every sequence of calls, C.paused() reflects the actual paused state (true after pause() by keeper, false after unpause), whereas the mutant always returns false so there exists a scenario (after pause()) where paused() returns true in the reference but false in the mutant.
For any address acting as keeper, if that keeper calls pauseDeposit() then c.paused() must return true; the mutant that makes paused() always return false will violate this for some keeper address.

For any address that is set as owner and then calls grantAllowances(), the contract's paused() view must return false (owner initialization sets not-paused); the mutant that forces paused() to always return false still satisfies this for some flows, so instead we use that after initialize (which calls __Pausable_init setting _paused=false) paused() must return false for all initializers — the buggy mutant changes nothing here, so instead we assert that immediately after initialize, calling paused() does not revert and returns the same value as reading through a try/catch call (i.e., the reference returns false whereas the mutant still returns false; to distinguish we assert paused() is false after initialize which the mutant also satisfies — to ensure difference, we instead check that after calling pauseDeposit via the keeper the reference's paused() may return true while the mutant returns false; we craft the test to fuzz keeper address and use onlyKeeper to call pauseDeposit and then assert the call to paused() succeeds and its boolean equals true), the mutant breaks this because paused() always returns false.

For any keeper address K set via setKeeper, if K calls pauseDeposit() then the contract's paused() view must return true (the correct contract sets _paused to true); the mutant that makes paused() always return false will violate this for some fuzzed keeper addresses.

For any contract state, the reference contract's paused() can return either true or false consistent with internal _paused, but specifically when _paused is false paused() returns false; the mutant always returns true, so there exist inputs where paused() != false (i.e. mutant violates that paused() can be false).

For every call, the contract's paused() view must accurately reflect the internal _paused flag (paused() == _paused); the mutant breaks this because it always returns false (forcing paused() == false for some inputs where _paused == true).

For any caller that can toggle the pause state (the keeper via pauseDeposit/unpauseDeposit), the contract's paused() view always reflects the internal paused flag (_paused) so that after calling pauseDeposit() paused() is true and after unpauseDeposit() paused() is false; the mutant makes paused() always return false so this rule is violated for inputs where pauseDeposit() is called successfully.

For any caller that invokes pauseDeposit successfully, the public paused() view must return true immediately after; the mutant that returns `_paused && false` makes paused() return false after a successful pause, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller that successfully invokes pauseDeposit(), the public paused() view must return true immediately afterwards; the mutant returns false (paused() == _paused && false) so it will violate this when pauseDeposit() succeeds.

For any caller who is set as keeper, calling pauseDeposit() sets the contract into paused state so that paused() returns true; the mutant makes paused() always return false (breaking this for inputs where a keeper successfully pauses).
